  • Is your child ready to stay home alone for a short time?
Baby & Child

Is your child ready to stay home alone for a short time?

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

You need to collect something nearby, and your child would rather finish drawing at home. Before deciding, try a question together: “If my phone goes to voicemail and you smell smoke, what would you do first?” Their answer can show which parts of the plan still need practice.

Look at readiness in this particular situation

Babies, toddlers and preschoolers need adult supervision. This decision is for an older child who can reliably follow the plan. Check the supervision requirements where you live. Think about your child’s age, judgement, communication needs and how they feel about the idea. Consider the time of day, the length of your absence and how quickly a trusted adult could reach them. A child able to spend a short time alone is not necessarily ready to supervise a sibling. Arrange adult care if they are frightened, need supervision or cannot get help reliably.

In a US survey, child protection specialists considered a hypothetical child left alone for four hours. Their judgements changed with the child’s age and the circumstances described. This was a study of professional opinions, not an experiment showing that four hours or any particular age is safe.

Rehearse with an adult still at home

Ask your child to demonstrate calling you and a nearby backup adult. Make sure they know their address and how to call local emergency services. Discuss an unexpected knock or phone call. They can keep the door closed, avoid revealing that they are alone and call the agreed adult. Practise leaving by a safe exit if there is smoke or a fire, staying out and calling emergency services from safety.

Agree on ordinary activities and limits. Set out a snack that needs no cooking, decide whether visitors are allowed and secure medicines, weapons, matches and other hazards. A charged phone should work from the place your child will use it. Do a pretend check-in and try the backup plan together.

Start briefly and revisit the decision

If local rules and your child’s readiness allow it, choose a short daytime absence with a nearby adult who has agreed to help. Set a return time and an exact check-in. If the check-in is missed and you cannot reach your child, arrange an immediate in-person check or return yourself. Seek emergency help if you believe the child is in danger.

Afterward, ask what went smoothly or felt uncomfortable. A chance to practise a familiar decision can build confidence, but staying alone is optional. Change the plan if your child asks for company or if the arrangements no longer fit.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check local supervision requirements.

Have the child demonstrate calling for help.

Keep a backup adult and clear return time.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests rehearsing what happens if the first call goes unanswered, then checking that the backup adult really is available.

When to seek help

If smoke or fire appears, leave by a safe exit, stay outside and call emergency services. If you cannot confirm your child is safe, arrange an immediate check and seek emergency help for actual or suspected danger.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Is your child ready to stay home alone?
  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Safety for children staying home on their own
  • Jennissen and colleagues, Injury Epidemiology — Professional judgements about a child left home alone

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check local requirements and the child’s readiness for this specific absence.
  • Rehearse calls, a closed-door response and the fire escape route.
  • Agree on a reachable backup adult, an end time and what happens after a missed check-in.

Frequently asked questions

What should a child know before being left alone?

They need a way to get help, their address, an emergency exit and the ability to follow the agreed plan. Practise together before you leave.

Which rules should we set?

Agree on visitors, the door, online contact, food, appliances and activities. Keep the first plan short enough to remember.

How can we try it for the first time?

Practise while an adult is home. If the child is willing and prepared and local rules allow it, begin briefly with a reachable adult nearby.

Are there benefits?

A child who is ready may enjoy practising an everyday decision independently. They can also practise independence while an adult stays close. There is no need to leave an unwilling child alone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
